title: Seabathers Eruption -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Seabather’s eruption, also referred to as "sea lice," is an intensely pruritic dermatitis that occurs after ocean exposure, most often in body areas covered by swimwear or subjected to friction. The condition results from contact with the nematocysts of marine cnidarians, primarily Linuche unguiculata (thimble jellyfish) and Edwardsiella lineata (sea anemone). Risk factors include swimming in tropical or subtropical coastal waters, prolonged exposure, tight-fitting swimwear, and delayed removal or rinsing of contaminated clothing.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Continuing Education Activity
content: The pathophysiology involves nematocyst discharge beneath swimwear or hair, releasing venom into the epidermis and triggering an acute inflammatory response. Lesions present as erythematous papules, vesicles, or urticarial plaques, accompanied by intense pruritus, typically localized to covered areas. Diagnosis is clinical, based on lesion distribution and recent marine exposure, with differential diagnoses including allergic contact dermatitis and cutaneous larva migrans.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Management is supportive, incorporating topical corticosteroids, oral antihistamines, and preventive measures such as prompt swimsuit removal. Complications are uncommon but may include increased cutaneous sensitivity and secondary bacterial infection. The prognosis is favorable, with resolution within 1 to 2 weeks and minimal risk of sequelae.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Introduction
content: Seabather’s eruption (SBE), also referred to as “sea lice,” is a pruritic dermatitis that occurs in a bathing suit distribution and at sites of friction following ocean exposure. The eruption is due to 2 saltwater cnidarian species: the thimble jellyfish ( Linuche unguiculata ) and the sea anemone ( Edwardsiella lineata ). [1] Both organisms are sufficiently small to become entrapped beneath swimwear. Pressure and exposure to freshwater trigger the discharge of nematocysts, specialized stinging organelles. Nematocysts release antigenic toxins that induce a host immune response.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Introduction
content: Larval-stage nematocysts of L unguiculata and E lineata elicit both types I and IV hypersensitivity reactions, producing the scattered pruritic red macules characteristic of SBE. [2] L unguiculata has been most commonly reported along the southeastern coast of the U.S., the Gulf of Mexico, and the Caribbean, with additional reports from Brazil and Papua New Guinea. [3] E lineata has been implicated in SBE along the U.S. East Coast, from the mid-Atlantic to New York. [4] Evidence suggests that other life stages of L unguiculata may also contribute to SBE.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Introduction
content: Incidence is highest during spring and summer, particularly in May and June. Children younger than 15 years are at elevated risk, likely due to increased exposure to the ocean. Surfers also exhibit an increased susceptibility, with lesions frequently occurring in areas of friction such as the chest, axilla, and abdomen. A prior history of SBE predisposes individuals to recurrent, more severe presentations. [5] [6] [7]

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Etiology
content: The nematocysts of L unguiculata and E lineata cause SBE. These organisms can become trapped beneath bathing suits after leaving the water. Pressure between the skin and swimwear triggers nematocyst discharge, resulting in envenomation by antigenic toxins. The toxins elicit a host immune response. [8]

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Epidemiology
content: Risk factors for SBE include age under 16 years, a prior history of the condition, and surfing activities. Children are at increased risk due to greater ocean exposure and more sensitive skin, while a history of SBE primes the immune system, leading to more intense reactions upon reexposure. Surfers are susceptible due to repeated friction in areas contacting nematocyst-laden water, which promotes venom discharge. [9]

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Pathophysiology
content: Nematocysts release venom containing phospholipase A2, which induces inflammation, and metalloproteases, which degrade proteins and inhibit coagulation. The resulting physiological effects include vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and impaired coagulation. [10]

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Histopathology
content: A biopsy is not required for diagnosis, and data on the histologic features of SBE are limited. When examined, histology resembles that of an arthropod bite, demonstrating a superficial and deep perivascular mixed infiltrate composed of neutrophils, lymphocytes, and eosinophils.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- History and Physical
content: The first symptom of SBE is pruritus or stinging, typically noted after leaving the water. A small number of patients may experience pruritus during ocean exposure. Freshwater can trigger nematocyst discharge. Therefore, patients who shower while wearing contaminated swimwear may report worsening symptoms after bathing. [11]

title: Seabathers Eruption -- History and Physical
content: SBE manifests as discrete, erythematous, pruritic papules that can progress to vesicles or pustules (see Image .  Seabather's Eruption). [12] Intense pruritus often leads to excoriation, which may obscure lesion identification and predispose to impetiginization. Lesions are primarily distributed beneath the bathing suit, with higher prevalence at sites of pressure such as the waistband. Additional lesions may appear at frictional sites, including the axilla, chest, and abdomen, in surfers. Patients with dense chest hair may also present with lesions in these areas. A recent case series suggested that SBE lesions arranged linearly may mimic the Koebner phenomenon, likely secondary to scratching, supporting the inclusion of SBE among diseases capable of triggering this event. [13]

title: Seabathers Eruption -- History and Physical
content: Lesions typically resolve within approximately 2 weeks but may persist for over a month in some cases. Systemic symptoms are rare but have included fever, malaise, nausea, vomiting, and cramps, usually lasting less than a week. A case of transient blurry vision associated with SBE has been reported, resolving without sequelae after a week.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- History and Physical
content: SBE is a clinical diagnosis. Biopsy and laboratory studies are generally unnecessary. In selected cases, titers for L unguiculata may remain positive several weeks postexposure or following reexposure. Recurrence can occur if contaminated swimwear is reused. Patients should be counseled to wash swimwear before subsequent use. [14]

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Evaluation
content: SBE is diagnosed clinically based on lesion morphology, distribution, and a history of ocean exposure. Laboratory studies, biopsy, and radiographic imaging are not useful for diagnosis. Serologic titers for L unguiculata are available, but a positive result only indicates prior exposure and is not diagnostic for SBE. Histologic examination, when performed, reveals a nonspecific superficial and deep mixed perivascular infiltrate that cannot be distinguished from an arthropod bite. A complete skin examination is recommended for patients with suspected SBE to assess lesion patterns, along with a detailed history of recent ocean swimming. Accurate diagnosis relies on a thorough history and focused physical examination.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Treatment / Management
content: Applying 5% acetic acid after leaving the water can inactivate any undischarged nematocysts. However, this intervention does not prevent the development of SBE. Most patients present after lesions have already formed.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Treatment / Management
content: Management is primarily symptomatic, utilizing systemic antihistamines and topical corticosteroids to reduce the inflammatory response. [15] Second-generation antihistamines, such as fexofenadine, may alleviate daytime pruritus, whereas diphenhydramine may be used at night when sedation is less of a concern.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Treatment / Management
content: Topical corticosteroids are commonly prescribed, with potency tailored to the site of the lesion. High-potency corticosteroids are avoided on the axilla, groin, and face because these areas carry a higher risk of adverse effects. Conversely, other body regions may be effectively treated with potent agents, such as clobetasol. Patients should also be counseled to wash swimwear with hot water and detergent to remove residual nematocysts and reduce the risk of recurrence.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of SBE includes arthropod bites, folliculitis, swimmer’s itch, seaweed dermatitis, diver dermatitis, and allergic contact dermatitis. Arthropod bites may be difficult to distinguish from SBE. However, the condition typically exhibits a different distribution and is associated with a history of outdoor rather than saltwater exposure. Grouped lesions, often in sets of 3 (the “breakfast, lunch, dinner” sign), are characteristic of arthropod bites. Folliculitis commonly affects the chest and back but may be more widespread. Lesions are predominantly pustular and may be at various stages of healing, which can aid differentiation from SBE; however, lesions with a bathing suit distribution may be challenging to distinguish.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Swimmer’s itch presents with pruritic erythematous papules similar to SBE but is caused by larval schistosomes that invade exposed skin, eliciting an immune response. Lesions are typically located on exposed areas. Exposure to freshwater lakes or rivers, rather than the ocean, helps differentiate swimmer’s itch from SBE. Seaweed dermatitis can mimic the appearance of SBE but results from fragments of seaweed trapped beneath swimwear. Exposure to seaweed blooms can support this diagnosis. Patients with sand-related exposures rather than seawater contact may have other parasitic infestations, such as scabies or cutaneous larva migrans. [16]

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis for SBE is excellent, as the condition is typically self-limited. Lesions generally resolve within several weeks without long-term sequelae. Management is primarily symptomatic, emphasizing pruritus relief and patient education to reduce the risk of recurrence. [17]

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Complications
content: Common complications of SBE include pruritus, which leads to excessive excoriation and secondary infections. As noted, previous SBE episodes prime the immune system and enhance cutaneous sensitivity, thereby increasing the risk of recurrence. Systemic symptoms resembling a mild flu-like illness, including fever, malaise, nausea, and vomiting, have been documented in SBE; however, the literature reports no cases of anaphylaxis.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: To help prevent SBE, swimmers should avoid ocean areas known to have high concentrations of jellyfish larvae during peak seasons, typically in late spring and early summer. [18] Wearing tight-fitting, smooth swimwear or wetsuits can reduce the chance of larvae becoming trapped under the fabric, as loose or porous clothing tends to hold more larvae. Minimizing the duration of swimwear contact while in the water and avoiding swimming in infested locations are also recommended.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Rinsing the skin with a 5% acetic acid solution may inactivate undischarged nematocysts, although this measure does not completely suppress the cutaneous reaction. Swimsuits should be washed thoroughly in hot water with detergent to remove any residual nematocysts and reduce the risk of recurrence.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: SBE is relatively common and best managed through an interprofessional approach that involves primary care physicians, emergency medicine physicians, dermatologists, nurses, and pharmacists. Primary care physicians provide initial assessment, symptomatic treatment, and patient education, while emergency medicine physicians evaluate acute or severe presentations and rule out mimicking conditions. Dermatologists are consulted for atypical, recurrent, or complicated cases and guide lesion care and preventive strategies. Management is primarily supportive, and most patients recover fully. Complete prevention is not possible except by avoiding exposure to the ocean.

title: Seabathers Eruption -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Swimwear should be removed promptly after swimming in the ocean. Patients should be informed that freshwater can trigger nematocyst discharge, which may exacerbate symptoms. Rinsing with freshwater may help wash away larvae trapped in clothing, but dilute acetic acid (vinegar) is preferred to inactivate nematocysts and reduce the severity of the eruption.
